subject: chemistry-hl
topicLabel: Structure 3.1 — Periodic table & electron structure (Nov unit)

items.stem: Which element is in group 17 and period 3?
items.note: Periods are rows, groups are columns: group 17 (halogens) + period 3 = chlorine. Fluorine is period 2.

items.stem: How many electrons are in the outer shell of any group 2 element?
items.note: Group number (1–18 s/p block) = number of outer-shell electrons for groups 1–2 and 13–18. Same valence count is why group members share chemistry.

items.stem: The full electron configuration of sodium (Z = 11) is:
items.note: Fill in aufbau order: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ (10 e⁻) then 3s¹ — the 11th electron enters 3s, not 3p.

items.stem: The condensed electron configuration of calcium (Z = 20) is:
items.note: 18 electrons fill up to argon; the remaining 2 go into 4s (4s fills before 3d). 3d² would be titanium.

items.stem: According to the aufbau principle, the sublevel filled immediately after 4s is:
items.note: Energy order: …3s 3p 4s 3d 4p. The 3d sublevel is filled after 4s — the source of most transition-metal configuration questions.

items.stem: The Pauli exclusion principle states that an orbital can hold:
choices: At most two electrons with opposite spins
items.note: Pauli: two electrons max per orbital, opposite spins. Hund's rule is the different principle about filling singly first.

items.stem: Nitrogen's 2p³ configuration has one electron in each 2p orbital. This illustrates:
items.note: Hund's rule: electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly before pairing — this extra stability explains the N→O ionization energy anomaly.

items.stem: Which ion has the same electron configuration as neon (Z = 10)?
items.note: Na⁺ = 11 − 1 = 10 electrons. K⁺ and Cl⁻ have 18 (argon-like); S²⁻ has 18 too. Count protons minus charge.

items.stem: Isotopes of the same element differ in their number of:
items.note: Same protons (that defines the element), different neutrons. Similar chemistry because electron configuration is unchanged.

items.stem: Moving across period 3 from Na to Cl, the atomic radius:
items.note: Electrons enter the same main shell while nuclear charge increases — greater pull, smaller radius. Down a group the radius increases (new shell).

items.stem: Going down group 2 from Mg to Ba, the first ionization energy:
items.note: New shell each period → outer electron farther away and more shielded → easier to remove. General downward trend, small local wobbles ignored at SL.

items.stem: The first ionization energy of boron is lower than that of beryllium because:
choices: The removed electron in B is in the higher-energy 2p sublevel
items.note: Be: 2s²; B: 2s²2p¹. The 2p electron is higher in energy and better shielded — easier to remove. This is the standard period 2 anomaly.

items.stem: The second ionization energy of sodium is much larger than the first because:
choices: The atom shrinks after the first ionization
The second electron is removed from the filled inner 2p shell
items.note: After losing 3s¹, Na⁺ has the stable 2p⁶ configuration; removing from an inner shell needs far more energy. Big IE jumps identify group numbers.

items.stem: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
items.note: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group — fluorine is the maximum on the Pauling scale.

items.stem: Which block of the periodic table contains iron (Fe)?
items.note: Transition metals fill d sublevels → d block. The block is determined by which sublevel the last electron enters.

items.stem: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have similar chemical properties because they have:
choices: The same number of valence electrons
items.note: Chemistry is governed by outer-shell electrons. Same shells alone would not group noble gases with alkali metals.

items.stem: The reactivity of group 1 metals with water:
choices: Is identical for all of them
items.note: Down group 1 the outer electron is farther and more shielded → lost more easily → more vigorous reaction. For group 17 halogens the trend is the opposite.

items.stem: Which oxide of a period 3 element is amphoteric?
items.note: Acid–basic character of oxides changes across the period: Na₂O/MgO basic, Al₂O₃ amphoteric, oxides of Si–Cl acidic. A favourite data-response question.

items.stem: Which statement about group 18 (noble gases) is correct?
choices: They have full outer shells and are generally unreactive
They are found in the s block
items.note: Full valence shells → high stability, low reactivity. Monatomic, and helium sits in the s block but the family property holds.

items.stem: How many valence electrons does a group 16 element have?
items.note: Groups 13–18: group number − 10 = valence electrons → 16 − 10 = 6 (oxygen family).

items.stem: Explain why the first ionization energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen.
markscheme: N has 2p³ — each 2p orbital singly occupied (half-filled, extra stability) (1)
O has 2p⁴ — the fourth electron must pair in an already-occupied orbital (1)
Electron–electron repulsion in the pair makes that electron easier to remove → lower IE for O (1)
items.tactic: IE anomalies: name the sublevel occupancy, invoke pairing/repulsion (O vs N) or sublevel energy (B vs Be). Two anomalies exist across period 2 — know both.

items.stem: An element X has successive ionization energies (kJ/mol): 577, 1816, 2744, 11577. Deduce the group of the periodic table to which X most likely belongs, giving a reason.
markscheme: Identify the very large jump between the 3rd and 4th ionization energies (1)
Three electrons removed with relatively low energy → three valence electrons (1)
The 4th electron comes from the inner, full shell — much harder to remove (1)
items.tactic: Successive IE problems: the position of the huge jump = number of valence electrons = group number. Draw the values as a bar chart if unsure.
